mainTopic: A wife's finds and surplus work, the husband's share in her בושת payment, and how a dowry is recorded in the כתובה
overview: The amud opens by finishing a challenge. If רבי עקיבא gives a wife the surplus of her handiwork, he should surely give her the things she finds. The גמרא answers by reversing the opinions, so רבי עקיבא gives her the find. רב פפא then explains that a find is like surplus produced through strain, which is exactly where רבי עקיבא and the רבנן disagree. Questions about a wife doing several tasks at once end with תיקו. Next, the גמרא asks why רבי יהודה בן בתירא lets a husband share in his wife's בושת payment. Through the examples of a horse, a garment and a noble family, it concludes that a wife counts as her husband's own self. A new משנה follows. A father-in-law need not give a pledged dowry to his dead son-in-law's brother. The same משנה then explains how a wife's dowry is recorded in the כתובה: cash is written higher, and appraised goods are written one-fifth lower.

steps.title: If surplus belongs to her, her finds surely should
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes a challenge: רבי עקיבא gives the wife the surplus of her handiwork, so he should surely give her the things she finds.
steps.simpleTranslation: Surplus is part of her handiwork, and still רבי עקיבא says it belongs to her. So the things she finds, which have nothing to do with her work, should belong to her all the more!
steps.whatsHappening: This line is the end of a challenge that began before this section. The גמרא is pointing out that a version where רבי עקיבא gives a wife's finds to her husband does not make sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Surplus comes from her handiwork, and the husband normally has rights to her handiwork. Even so, רבי עקיבא gives the surplus to her. A find is not connected to her work at all, so the husband's claim to it should be weaker. This is a כל שכן argument.

keyTerms.meaning: Her handiwork; what she earns from her work, which normally goes to her husband
Her find; a lost object she picked up
To herself; it belongs to her
All the more so; an argument from the stronger case

phrases.english: which is her handiwork,
phrases.notes: 'Which' means the surplus (העדפה) mentioned earlier in the sentence.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said it belongs to her —
her find, all the more so, no?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a challenge that began before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: A version in which רבי עקיבא gives a wife's finds to her husband
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רבי עקיבא gives her the surplus, which comes from her handiwork, then he should surely give her the finds, which do not come from her handiwork.

steps.title: Source showing רבי עקיבא gives surplus to the wife
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה in נדרים to prove that רבי עקיבא holds surplus belongs to the wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: if a wife says, 'Whatever I make is forbidden like a קרבן to your mouth,' the husband does not need to cancel the vow. רבי עקיבא says he should cancel it, in case she produces more than she owes him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports the claim inside its challenge by showing where רבי עקיבא says surplus belongs to the wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ת"ק holds the vow has no effect, because she cannot forbid what she must make for him. רבי עקיבא worries she will produce extra beyond what she owes. The vow could take hold on that extra, so the extra must be hers.

keyTerms.meaning: A vow word that makes something forbidden like a קרבן
To cancel a vow, which a husband can do for his wife
She will produce extra, beyond what she owes
What is fitting for him; what he is owed

phrases.english: As we learned in a mishna:
"What I make is konam to your mouth" —
he does not need to nullify it.
Rabbi Akiva says: He should nullify it,
lest she produce extra for him
beyond what is fitting for him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the premise of the challenge in Step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא holds a wife's surplus belongs to her
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in נדרים about a vow of קונם on her handiwork

steps.title: Reverse the opinions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers by switching the opinions: the first opinion gives a wife's find to her husband, and רבי עקיבא gives it to her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, reverse the opinions: a wife's find belongs to her husband. רבי עקיבא says it belongs to her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem by switching who said what about a wife's finds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the switch, רבי עקיבא gives her both the surplus and the find, so he no longer contradicts himself. The first opinion gives the find to the husband.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; this introduces a new approach
Reverse; switch the opinions
To her husband

phrases.english: Rather, reverse it:
A wife's find belongs to her husband.
Rabbi Akiva says: To herself.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the order. After the reversal, רבי עקיבא is the one who gives the find to the wife.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Steps 1 and 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא gives a wife's find to her husband, which contradicts his view on surplus.
steps.terutzMaskana: Switch the opinions: רבי עקיבא gives the find to the wife.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן limits רבי עקיבא's view on surplus
steps.stepSummary: Through רבין, רבי יוחנן says that ordinary surplus goes to the husband according to everyone. רבי עקיבא gives her only surplus produced through extra strain.
steps.simpleTranslation: But when רבין came, he reported that רבי יוחנן said: surplus that came without strain belongs to the husband according to everyone. They disagree only about surplus produced through strain. The ת"ק says it goes to the husband, and רבי עקיבא says it goes to her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reversal. It brings רבי יוחנן's teaching that רבי עקיבא gives her the surplus only in a limited case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבי עקיבא agrees that ordinary surplus goes to the husband, the כל שכן argument breaks down. A find might be like ordinary surplus, so there was no need to reverse the opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: When רבין came from ארץ ישראל to Babylonia with teachings
Surplus; extra work beyond what she owes
Through strain; through unusual effort
Everyone agrees
The first opinion in the משנה, the ת"ק

phrases.english: But when Ravin came,
he reported that Rabbi Yochanan said:
With surplus that comes without strain —

phrases.aramaic: כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דְּבַעַל הָוֵי.
phrases.english: everyone agrees that it belongs to the husband.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי פְּלִיגִי בְּהַעְדָּפָה שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַדְּחָק:
phrases.english: Where they disagree is surplus that comes through strain:
the first tanna holds it belongs to her husband,
and Rabbi Akiva holds it belongs to her.

steps.kashyaTarget: The reversal in Step 3 and the כל שכן argument behind it
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי עקיבא gives her only surplus produced through strain. A find might be like ordinary surplus, which goes to the husband, so the כל שכן argument does not work and the reversal is not needed.

steps.title: A find is like surplus produced through strain
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says a wife's find counts like surplus produced through strain, so the reversed dispute stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: her find is like surplus produced through strain. It falls under the dispute between רבי עקיבא and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge by putting a find in the same group as surplus produced through strain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Finding something is unusual, like working with extra strain. So רבי עקיבא gives it to her, and the רבנן give it to the husband. This keeps the reversed version from Step 3.

keyTerms.meaning: It is like; it is comparable
A dispute
The Rabbis; here, the first opinion against רבי עקיבא

steps.whatToRemember: A wife's find is treated like surplus produced through strain. רבי עקיבא gives it to her, and the רבנן give it to her husband.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Her find is like surplus
that comes through strain.
It is the dispute of Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: מְצִיאָתָהּ כְּהַעְדָּפָה שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַדְּחָק דָּמֵי
steps.terutzResolutionType: Putting the find in the right category
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A find might be like ordinary surplus, which everyone gives to the husband.
steps.terutzMaskana: A find is like surplus produced through strain, so it is part of the dispute, and the reversal stands.

steps.title: Two tasks done at the same time
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks what the law is if the wife did two tasks for her husband at the same time.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא asked: if she did two tasks for him at once, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא asks a new question that comes out of the idea of surplus produced through strain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Doing two jobs at once creates extra output. The question is whether that counts as surplus produced through strain, which רבי עקיבא gives to her, or as ordinary surplus, which goes to the husband.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked; he raised an open question
What is the law?
At the same time
Two

phrases.english: Rav Pappa asked:

phrases.aramaic: עָשְׂתָה לוֹ שְׁתַּיִם בְּבַת אַחַת, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: If she did two for him at once, what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'Two' means two tasks, like doing two kinds of work at the same time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the idea of strain from Steps 4 and 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether two tasks done at once count as surplus produced through strain

steps.title: Three or four tasks done at the same time
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks the same question about three or four tasks done at once.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא asked: if she did three or four at once, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא pushes רב פפא's question further, to more tasks at once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if two tasks at once is not considered strain, three or four at once might be. רבינא wants to know where the line is.

keyTerms.meaning: Three or four

phrases.english: Ravina asked:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלֹשָׁה אוֹ אַרְבָּעָה בְּבַת אַחַת, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: Three or four at once, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends רב פפא's question in Step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether three or four tasks at once count as surplus produced through strain

steps.title: The questions stay unresolved
steps.stepSummary: Both questions are left unanswered with תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand; the questions are not resolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends both questions without an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source settles whether doing several tasks at once counts as strain. Both questions remain open.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question stays unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: The cases of two tasks at once and of three or four tasks at once are left unresolved (תיקו).

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the questions in Steps 6 and 7.

steps.title: Would humiliating someone's horse require a humiliation payment?
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב חנן attacks רבי יהודה בן בתירא's view that the husband shares in his wife's בושת payment, using the example of a horse.
steps.simpleTranslation: Her humiliation and her degradation. רבא בר רב חנן objected: If so, if someone humiliated another person's horse, would he also have to pay the owner for humiliation?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words about a wife's בושת and פגם. Then רבא בר רב חנן challenges the opinion that the husband gets part of that money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה בן בתירא seems to give the husband a share because something that belongs to him was shamed. If so, shaming any of a man's possessions, like his horse, should also earn him a בושת payment. That sounds ridiculous, so the reasoning looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Payment for humiliation
Payment for the drop in her value, her 'degradation'
He strongly objected to it
But if so (introduces a strange result of your logic)

phrases.english: Her humiliation and her degradation.
phrases.notes: These words are quoted from the משנה. There, רבי יהודה בן בתירא says the husband gets part of this money.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רָבָא בַּר רַב חָנָן:
phrases.english: Rava bar Rav Chanan strongly objected to it:
But if so,
if one humiliated his fellow's horse,

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי נָמֵי דְּבָעֵי לְמִיתַּן לֵיהּ בּוֹשֶׁת?
phrases.english: would he also be required to give him payment for humiliation?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רָבָא בַּר רַב חָנָן: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the questions about extra work to the next clause of the משנה, the payments for בושת and פגם.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה בן בתירא's ruling that the husband shares in his wife's בושת payment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reductio: if shaming a man's 'possession' earns him בושת, then shaming his horse should too.

steps.title: A horse cannot feel humiliation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the horse comparison, because a horse cannot be humiliated at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: But can a horse be humiliated?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against its own example. A horse feels no shame, so it cannot be compared to a wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wife really is humiliated, so there is real shame here. A horse has no shame at all. The comparison fails, so the challenge needs a better example.

keyTerms.meaning: Capable of being humiliated

phrases.english: And is a horse capable of humiliation?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the example used in step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the horse example, not the whole challenge
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A horse has no capacity for shame, unlike a person.

steps.title: Would spitting on someone's clothing require a humiliation payment?
steps.stepSummary: The challenge is restated with a better example: spitting on a person's garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if someone spat on another person's clothing, would he also have to pay for humiliation?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rebuilds the challenge using a garment instead of a horse. Spitting on a garment does insult its owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a garment there is a real person who could feel insulted, so the horse problem goes away. If the husband collects because 'his' wife was shamed, then the owner of a spat-on garment should collect too.

keyTerms.meaning: He spat
His garment

phrases.english: Rather: if one spat on his fellow's garment,

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי נָמֵי דְּבָעֵי לְמִיתַּן לֵיהּ בּוֹשֶׁת?
phrases.english: would he also be required to give him payment for humiliation?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected horse example with a garment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If shaming what belongs to a man earns him בושת, then spitting on his garment should earn it too.

steps.title: A משנה shows that spitting on a garment earns no payment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves from a משנה, as explained by רב פפא, that spitting on a garment carries no בושת payment, which sharpens the challenge.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that yes, he would pay, we learned: If he spat and the spit reached him, or uncovered a woman's head, or pulled off someone's cloak, he must pay four hundred זוז. And רב פפא said: This is only when it reached him, but if it reached his garment, he is exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks a way out. Someone might say spitting on a garment really does require payment. A משנה, read by רב פפא, shows it does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Spitting that touches the person costs four hundred זוז. Spitting that only touches his garment costs nothing. So shaming a man's belongings earns him no בושת money, and the husband's share looks harder to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say
Uncovered a woman's head (a serious public shaming)
They only taught this when
Exempt from paying

phrases.english: And if you would say, yes, indeed, but didn't we learn:
If he spat and the spit reached him,
or he uncovered a woman's head,
or he removed his cloak from him,

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּיב לִיתֵּן לוֹ אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת זוּז.
phrases.english: he must give him four hundred zuz.
And Rav Pappa said:
They taught this only when it reached him himself,
but if it reached his garment, he is exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the challenge of step 11 by showing that the garment case really carries no payment.
steps.raayaObject: That shaming a person's belongings, like his garment, carries no בושת payment
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in בבא קמא together with רב פפא's explanation

steps.title: A wife's shame disgraces her husband, a garment's does not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a garment being spat on brings no real disgrace, but a wife's humiliation truly disgraces her husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: With his garment, there is no disgrace to him. With his wife, there is disgrace.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by explaining why a wife is different from a garment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband's share does not come from her being 'his property.' It comes from the real disgrace he feels when his wife is shamed. Spit on a garment does not disgrace its owner like that.

keyTerms.meaning: Disgrace, dishonor
He does not have
There is for her (she has)

phrases.english: With his garment, he has no disgrace;
his wife, there is disgrace in her case.
phrases.notes: He means that her shame reflects on her husband too, so he is shamed through her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the garment challenge of steps 11 and 12.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The husband shares because something of his was shamed, like a garment.
steps.terutzMaskana: The husband shares because his wife's shame truly disgraces him, which a garment's does not.

steps.title: Would a whole noble family collect for one relative's shame?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא challenges the answer: when a poor man from a noble family is shamed, his whole family is disgraced, so should they all be paid?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: If so, if someone humiliated a poor man from a noble family, where all the family members are disgraced, would he have to pay all of them for humiliation?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא attacks the answer of step 13. If disgrace alone earns payment, then relatives who feel disgraced should also collect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 said the husband collects because he feels disgraced. But relatives of a noble family also feel disgraced when one of them is shamed. Nobody pays a whole family, so 'disgrace' alone cannot be the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: A poor man from a noble, respected family
Family members

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, בִּיֵּישׁ עָנִי בֶּן טוֹבִים,
phrases.english: But if so, if one humiliated a poor man of a noble family,
where there is disgrace
for all the family members,

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי נָמֵי דְּבָעֵי לְמִיתַּן לְהוּ בּוֹשֶׁת
phrases.english: would he also be required to give them payment for humiliation,
to all the family members?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the husband collects because of the disgrace he feels
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Relatives also feel disgraced, yet they surely do not each collect בושת.

steps.title: A wife is like her husband's own self
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that relatives are separate people, but a wife counts as part of her husband himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, the relatives are not themselves the ones shamed. Here, his wife is like his own self.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי explains why the husband collects but other relatives do not. A wife is treated as one with her husband.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A relative's shame touches the family only indirectly, so they do not collect. A wife is considered her husband's own body, so shaming her is like shaming him directly. That is why he shares in the payment.

keyTerms.meaning: His own body, himself
A wife is like her husband's own self (the idea behind this answer)

steps.whatToRemember: The husband's share in his wife's בושת payment comes from her being like 'his own self.' It is not because she belongs to him like a garment or a horse. It is also not just because he is disgraced, the way relatives are.

phrases.english: He said to him: There, it is not their own selves;
here, his wife is his own self.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any disgrace felt by a relative should earn a payment.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a wife, who counts as her husband's own self, makes him a partner in her בושת payment.

steps.title: New משנה: A dowry pledge does not pass to the groom's brother
steps.stepSummary: A father-in-law pledged money to his son-in-law, who then died. He can refuse to give it to the brother.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone pledged money to his son-in-law and the son-in-law died, the חכמים said he can say: I wanted to give to your brother, but I don't want to give to you.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. A father pledged a dowry to his son-in-law, and the son-in-law died. The father does not have to give that money to the dead man's brother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The promise was made to one specific person. When the brother steps in to marry the widow, the promise does not move over to him. The father can say he never meant to give it to this man.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (marks the start of a new משנה)
One who pledges or sets an amount
His son-in-law
I do not want

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who pledges money to his son-in-law,
and his son-in-law died,
the Sages said:
he can say:
To your brother I wanted to give,
phrases.notes: He is talking to the dead groom's brother, who comes to marry the widow through יבום.

phrases.english: but to you I do not want to give.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dowry pledged to a son-in-law who died does not have to be given to his brother.

steps.title: Cash dowry gets written higher, appraised goods get written one-fifth lower
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that for a cash dowry of 1,000 dinars the husband writes 1,500 in the כתובה, but for appraised goods he writes one-fifth less than the appraisal.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the bride pledged to bring her husband 1,000 dinars, he writes 1,500 for it in the כתובה. For goods that were appraised, he writes one-fifth less than their appraised value.
steps.whatsHappening: The same משנה moves on to a second topic: how the dowry the wife brings is recorded in her כתובה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Cash is the most useful thing a husband can receive, since he can do business with it. So he writes a larger sum than she gave. Goods like clothing and utensils are usually appraised above their true value, so he writes one-fifth less than the appraisal.

keyTerms.meaning: She pledged or committed (to bring a certain dowry)
He commits a matching amount in the כתובה
A unit of money equal to 100 dinars
An appraisal: goods given a money value
One-fifth less

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two directions. For cash the husband writes MORE than he received. For appraised goods he writes LESS than the appraisal.

phrases.english: If she pledged to bring in for him a thousand dinars,

phrases.aramaic: הוּא פּוֹסֵק כְּנֶגְדָּן חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מָנֶה,
phrases.english: he pledges against them fifteen maneh,
phrases.notes: A מנה is 100 dinars, so this is 1,500 dinars.

phrases.aramaic: וּכְנֶגֶד הַשּׁוּם הוּא פּוֹסֵק פָּחוֹת חוֹמֶשׁ.
phrases.english: and against the appraisal he pledges one-fifth less.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה as step 16, moving from the father-in-law's pledge to how the wife's dowry is recorded in the כתובה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A cash dowry is recorded in the כתובה at one and a half times its amount. An appraised dowry is recorded at one-fifth less than the appraisal.

steps.title: When the appraisal matches the true value
steps.stepSummary: If goods were appraised at 100 and are truly worth 100, the husband is credited with only 100.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the goods were appraised at 100 dinars and really are worth 100, he only has 100.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה looks at a special case where the appraisal was done at the real market value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The one-fifth reduction exists only because appraisals usually run high. When the appraisal equals the true value, there is nothing to take off, so the full 100 counts.

keyTerms.meaning: Worth: the real value of the item
He has only

phrases.english: An appraisal at a maneh, and it is worth a maneh,
he has only a maneh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Qualifies the one-fifth rule from step 17 for a case where the appraisal is exact.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the appraised value equals the true value, the husband's credit is exactly that value.

steps.title: Number examples of the one-fifth rule
steps.stepSummary: For the husband to write 100 in the כתובה, she must give goods appraised at 125. For him to write 400, she must give goods appraised at 500.
steps.simpleTranslation: For an appraisal of 100 to be written, she gives 31 סלע and a dinar (125 dinars). For 400 to be written, she gives 500. What...
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה shows the one-fifth rule with actual numbers. The last word, מה, starts a new sentence that continues in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking one-fifth off 125 leaves 100, and taking one-fifth off 500 leaves 400. So the goods she brings must be appraised one-quarter higher than the sum he writes.

keyTerms.meaning: A coin worth 4 dinars
She gives (brings in as dowry)

steps.whatToRemember: Written amount = appraisal minus one-fifth. So 125 becomes 100, and 500 becomes 400.

phrases.english: For an appraisal of a maneh,
phrases.notes: He means the 100 that the husband writes in the כתובה.

phrases.aramaic: הִיא נוֹתֶנֶת שְׁלֹשִׁים וְאֶחָד סֶלַע וְדִינָר.
phrases.english: she gives thirty-one sela and a dinar.
phrases.notes: A סלע is 4 dinars, so 31 סלע plus 1 dinar is 125 dinars.

phrases.english: And for four hundred, she gives five hundred.
